title: KML Viewer: Placemarks, Paths and Polygons
description: Open a KML or KMZ file and see its placemarks, paths and polygons in the browser with the KML Viewer — parsed locally, nothing uploaded. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a council's KMZ of proposed cycle lanes unzips in the browser and draws every route and zone — no Google Earth install, no upload, just the map the file describes.
quick_answer: The KML Viewer draws a KML or KMZ file's placemarks, paths and polygons on a map, entirely in your browser. Drop the file and inspect what it contains — geometry, names and structure — before it goes into a GIS, a presentation or the ground.
steps_intro: KML files promise maps. This one shows the map:

body.t: KML arrives from planners, councils and clients who assume Earth is installed. The viewer opens it anywhere — and the
sizes it first if it looks huge.
What you exported is what they will see: polygons closed, paths in the right county, labels attached. Thirty seconds here prevents the recall email.
A boundary or route file becomes a shareable picture for a meeting — screenshot the view, keep the file itself for the record.
A decade of KML in a shared drive becomes browsable. Files that draw nothing, or draw in the ocean, announce themselves instantly.

examples.label: Example · The polygon in the sea

body.t: A site boundary drawn offshore means coordinates were written lat,lon into a format that demands lon,lat. KML's order is the single most common cause — the viewer makes the error visible, the source system must fix it.

examples.label: Example · KMZ is a zip, not a mystery

body.t: A KMZ is KML plus its assets in a zip archive (doc.kml inside). The viewer opens the package directly; counters that ask for 'the KML' mean the doc.kml within.

popular_table.note: Advanced Earth features (3D Models, photo tours, gx:Tracks) are simplified or skipped by a 2D web viewer — stated plainly so their absence is expected, not alarming.

faq: Yes — the viewer unpacks the archive in the browser and draws the doc.kml inside, with its bundled icons and images where the file provides them.
My polygons have no fill colour.
KML styling lives in <Style> elements; unstyled geometry draws with defaults. Missing styles are a file property, not a viewer failure.
Labels come from each Placemark's <name>. The Named Placemark Counter audits exactly that coverage.
Links to remote KML are not fetched and executed blindly — load the linked file itself if you need its contents. A deliberate safety posture.
Can I edit in the viewer?
Viewing is read-only by design. Edits belong to Earth or a GIS, where change tracking exists.
The file draws but in the wrong place entirely.
Datum surprises are rare in KML (it is WGS84 by specification); axis order is the usual culprit — see the sea-polygon example.
Screenshot it — the picture is the portable artefact; the file remains the data of record.
